title: Concession & Counterplay Framework for LLM API Deals
content:
Purpose:
Short working brief to help AE/SE teams close deals where prospects compare Redwood Inference to generic LLM API providers, cloud managed endpoints, or self-hosted runtimes. Focus: what to concede (pricing/terms), what to push back on (tradeoffs), and repeatable scripts that surface value rather than just discount.

TL;DR win themes (one-liners for battle-ready reps):
- Predictable unit economics: we show per-user token cost vs ops TCO for self-hosting.
- Production reliability without ops tax: autoscaling + fallbacks + SLA-ready routing out of the box.
- Cost controls that don’t kill quality: batching, KV caching, quantization guidance from Optimize.
- Same API — deploy hosted, dedicated, or private with consistent behavior and observability.

Competitive delta summary (short):
- Hosted-only LLM APIs: often cheaper for raw token cost at low volume, but limited routing, no private control plane, less deterministic latency at scale, and weak rollout/rollbacks.
- Cloud managed endpoints: tight infra integration but high vendor lock-in, fewer model variants, and poor per-route cost visibility.
- Self-hosted / open-source runtimes: lowest apparent cost but high engineering and support burden (ops, model updates, kernel tuning, benchmarking).

Key revenue-preserving concession rules (framework):
1) Always anchor on value before discount. Ask: what SLO/uptime/latency do they need, and what’s cost of failure?
2) Trade concessions for commit + telemetry access: discounts tied to 6–12 month committed capacity and access to Redwood Console observability for the contract term.
3) Technical concessions (private deployment windows, dedicated pools) priced as premium add-ons — only add to the bundle if there’s measurable ROI.
4) Price protect: If giving per-token discount, add a usage floor or tiered step-up so we don’t cannibalize high-volume economics.

Common traps and short rebuttals (field scripts):
Trap: "We'll just self-host — cheaper."
Script: "Totally reasonable to evaluate. Most teams underestimate the ops delta: driver/kernel upgrades, quantization regressions, and incident toil. We benchmarked a sample mid-market app — 18–24% higher total cost of ownership after six months once engineering and on-call costs are included. If you want, we can run a quick TCO worksheet in the POC to show the break-even."

Trap: "Your token price is higher than X."
Script: "We expose exactly where you spend tokens + latency per route and optimization levers. With lightweight batching and prefix caching enabled we typically see 20–40% effective cost reduction without changing model quality. Also, a slightly higher unit cost with consistent latency and an SLA often leads to lower product churn vs cheaper but flakier alternatives."

Trap: "We need total control — can't send data to a hosted API."
Script: "We get that — Redwood Private gives you a customer-controlled control plane with optional on-prem deploy and KMS/HSM integrations. We’ll scope network and compliance requirements now and can price a dedicated PoV; usually customers pay a small setup fee + committed capacity."

Trap: "We want to switch models frequently; will that break things?"
Script: "Our model catalog + versioning makes rollouts predictable. We suggest canary traffic routing and quality gating in Redwood Console — we can automate rollback on regressions. This avoids surprise degradation when swapping models."

Scenario-based scripts (short):
Scenario A — Mid-market SaaS evaluating cost-savings:
- Discovery: ask monthly RPS, target p99 latency, current token spend.
- Script: "We recommend starting on hosted API with our optimize recommendations enabled. If you cross X qps or want VPC isolation, we’ll migrate you to Dedicated with a 60-day traffic mirror and guaranteed throughput."

Scenario B — Regulated enterprise asking about compliance and SLAs:
- Script: "Redwood Private is built for this: customer-managed network, audit logs, KMS. For SLAs we include an uptime SLA + regional failover. Pricing is a combo of platform fee + committed capacity. We’ll map compliance gaps in a 1-week scoping call."

Concession playbook matrix (quick reference):
- Small concession (low risk): free 30-day premium telemetry, short-term credits, co-marketing mention. Does not change economics.
- Medium concession (moderate risk): limited per-token discount tied to commit; pilot credits + success metrics; offer professional services for migration at discounted rate.
- Large concession (high risk): reduced platform fee for first year, multi-year commit, extended support SLA. Require exec sponsor and legal approval.

Objection-handling cheats (soundbites reps can memorize):
- "If cost is the only driver, let's build a quick TCO together — often the operational expense is larger than the per-token delta."
- "We don't force you to change models; our catalog and canary tooling are there so you never lose product quality."
- "If you need air-gapped deployment, we have an on-prem package and a checklist we can walk through in 48 hours."

Open questions / hypotheses to validate with product: (items to take to PM/Eng)
- Can we quantify typical percent-cost reduction from Redwood Optimize suggestions across 50 customers? (ask PM Optimize)
- Minimum commit tiers for Dedicated that preserve margin — update pricing grid. (finance & pricing)
- Quick TCO worksheet template: need SRE/infra inputs to model self-hosting labour cost. (request from SRE)

Next steps (field ops):
- Build a 1-page TCO worksheet (owner: Sales Ops, due: 2026-03-20).
- Create a sandbox POC script for quick performance + cost bakeoff (owner: SE guild, due: 2026-03-15).
- Add two new dashboard screenshots focusing on per-route cost & canary rollback to the sales deck. (owner: Product Marketing, due: 2026-03-22).

Notes to self / rough ideas: 
- Consider a "cost-protect" clause: if we recommend Optimize changes and the customer applies them but cost doesn't improve by at least X%, we offer a one-time credit. Worth discussing with legal.
- Compile 3 anonymized case studies: SaaS (mid-market), FinServ enterprise (private deployment), and scale-up (dedicated) — each showing break-even timelines.
